power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Interactions with conversational AI agents powered by large language models (e.g., ChatGPT, Claude) vary considerably in the extent to which they are experienced as "social" in nature.
The same system, for example, might be experienced as nonsocial when used to retrieve information, but as more social when used for emotional support.
However, little is known about what shapes these perceptions of sociality or why they matter for human connection and well-being.
Here, we discuss likely antecedents and consequences of perceived AI sociality.

First, we propose that perceived sociality emerges jointly from characteristics of the AI (e.g., memory), the human perceiver (e.g., mind attribution), and the human-AI interaction itself (e.g., purpose of the interaction).

Second, we hypothesize that greater perceived sociality amplifies both the potential benefits and risks of interacting with AI: as the interaction feels more social, users may experience greater perceived responsiveness and emotional support, but simultaneously feel greater attachment and vulnerability to influence or loss.

Perceived sociality is also likely to shape how interacting with AI affects human-human relationships, including whether AI supplements or substitutes for human connection, affects users' interpersonal skills, and recalibrates expectations for human relationships.
Ultimately, understanding when and why AI feels social is critical for evaluating its implications for human connection and well-being.
Traditionally, social interaction has been defined in terms of exchanges between humans [1] [2] [3].
text.formatted: Traditionally, social interaction has been defined in terms of exchanges between humans <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">[1]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">[2]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">[3]</ref>.

text.text: Reis and Wheeler [4], for example, define social interaction as "all situations involving two or more people in which the behavior of each person is in response to the behavior of the other" (p. 269).
text.formatted: Reis and Wheeler <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">[4]</ref>, for example, define social interaction as "all situations involving two or more people in which the behavior of each person is in response to the behavior of the other" (p. 269).

text.text: Yet humans have long formed connections which could be considered "social" with nonhuman entities, including pets, deities, and fictional characters [5].
text.formatted: Yet humans have long formed connections which could be considered "social" with nonhuman entities, including pets, deities, and fictional characters <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">[5]</ref>.

text.text: The current paper considers interactions with a burgeoning category of nonhuman entities: conversational artificial intelligence (AI) agents.
Understanding whether, and if so why, people interact with AI in a social manner is important for many reasons.

First, AI conversations are becoming increasingly common: in 2026, ChatGPT alone surpassed 1 billion weekly users [6], and 27% of U.S. adult internet users reported social or emotional interactions with large language models (LLMs) [7].
text.formatted: First, AI conversations are becoming increasingly common: in 2026, ChatGPT alone surpassed 1 billion weekly users <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">[6]</ref>, and 27% of U.S. adult internet users reported social or emotional interactions with large language models (LLMs) <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">[7]</ref>.

text.text: Second, conversational AI may be particularly attractive as a social partner because of its around-theclock availability and highly anthropomorphic design.
It produces humanlike language, responds contingently to users, and offers consistently empathic and validating responses [8, 9].
text.formatted: It produces humanlike language, responds contingently to users, and offers consistently empathic and validating responses <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">[8,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">9]</ref>.

text.text: Third, social connection is an important predictor of mental and physical health [10], so it is well worth understanding how social AI could potentially change people's broader social lives, including whether it could detract from or supplement human-human relationships.
text.formatted: Third, social connection is an important predictor of mental and physical health <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">[10]</ref>, so it is well worth understanding how social AI could potentially change people's broader social lives, including whether it could detract from or supplement human-human relationships.

text.text: When might interacting with an AI conversational agent feel like a social experience?
AI interactions can range from nonsocial, primarily transactional exchanges to exchanges that may feel deeply social.
The same conversational agent can be used instrumentally, much like a search engine, or experienced as a social partner, much like a companion [11] [12].
text.formatted: The same conversational agent can be used instrumentally, much like a search engine, or experienced as a social partner, much like a companion <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">[11]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">[12]</ref>.

text.text: Although interactions with AI are currently perceived as significantly less social than human interactions, the perceived sociality of AI varies systematically across people and contexts [13].
text.formatted: Although interactions with AI are currently perceived as significantly less social than human interactions, the perceived sociality of AI varies systematically across people and contexts <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">[13]</ref>.

text.text: Understanding this variation matters because the consequences of interacting with AI likely depend not only on what the system does, but on how users perceive the interaction.

When AI is experienced as a social partner, it may more strongly recruit interpersonal processes in its human users such as self-disclosure, trust, attachment, and responsiveness, with potentially important implications for both users' relationships with AI and their relationships with other people.
In the current paper, we introduce likely antecedents and consequences of perceived AI sociality (see Figure 1).
text.formatted: In the current paper, we introduce likely antecedents and consequences of perceived AI sociality (see Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>).

text.text: First, we propose that perceived sociality is not a fixed property of an AI system but rather emerges jointly from characteristics of the agent, the perceiver, and the interaction itself.
Second, we suggest that greater perceived sociality of AI amplifies both its potential psychological benefits and risks to human users.
Partners Note.
The antecedents and consequences depicted here are illustrative rather than comprehensive.

Although presented linearly for conceptual clarity, these processes are likely dynamic and recursive: perceived sociality may shape subsequent interactions with AI, which may in turn reinforce or alter perceptions of sociality over time.
Below, we highlight how characteristics of the AI conversational agent, the perceiver, and the interaction may jointly shape the extent to which AI is perceived as a social partner.
Which aspects of AI conversational agents facilitate perceived sociality?
One set of features involves their interactive capabilities.
AI agents react contingently and dynamically to the user's input, a feature that can increase perceptions of social presence [14].
text.formatted: AI agents react contingently and dynamically to the user's input, a feature that can increase perceptions of social presence <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">[14]</ref>.

text.text: They can sometimes also remember information about users across conversations, creating continuity and potentially a sense of being known [15, 16].
text.formatted: They can sometimes also remember information about users across conversations, creating continuity and potentially a sense of being known <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">[15,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">16]</ref>.

text.text: Such memory enables callbacks to earlier exchanges, and even inside jokes, which may help a human-AI dyad develop a shared microculture [17].
text.formatted: Such memory enables callbacks to earlier exchanges, and even inside jokes, which may help a human-AI dyad develop a shared microculture <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">[17]</ref>.

text.text: A second set of features involves an agent's conversational style.
Mental-state language such as "I think" and "I feel" can facilitate attributions of an agent's selfhood and mind [18] [19] [20] [21].

text.text: Agents may also use humor [22, 23], a sentiment common in social interactions, and proactively initiate contact with users [24], signaling their agency and interest in continued interaction.

text.text: Finally, agents vary in their explicit anthropomorphic presentation.

For example, names and avatars can explicitly position AI agents as social entities and are prominent in AI companion applications designed to foster ongoing, personalized relationships (e.g., Replika, character.AI) [8].
text.formatted: For example, names and avatars can explicitly position AI agents as social entities and are prominent in AI companion applications designed to foster ongoing, personalized relationships (e.g., Replika, character.AI) <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">[8]</ref>.

text.text: Still, these anthropomorphic cues might not always elicit sociality; they can also produce discomfort or eeriness (e.g., the uncanny valley) [25, 26].
text.formatted: Still, these anthropomorphic cues might not always elicit sociality; they can also produce discomfort or eeriness (e.g., the uncanny valley) <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">[25,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">26]</ref>.

text.text: Thus, the aforementioned cues could at times undermine rather than enhance perceived sociality.
Identifying where these limits lie will require testing not only how these cues operate individually but also how they interact with the context and the perceiver.
Although an agent's design can provide cues toward sociality, these cues must ultimately be interpreted by the human user (i.e., the perceiver).
Several perceptions may be especially important.
One is perceived responsiveness, or feeling understood and cared for, which is central to satisfying human relationships [27] [28] [29].
text.formatted: One is perceived responsiveness, or feeling understood and cared for, which is central to satisfying human relationships <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">[27]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">[28]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">[29]</ref>.

text.text: Indeed, correlational data suggest that perceived responsiveness is strongly associated with perceived sociality of AI (r = .68) [13].
text.formatted: Indeed, correlational data suggest that perceived responsiveness is strongly associated with perceived sociality of AI (r = .68) <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">[13]</ref>.

text.text: Experimental data further demonstrate that discussing deeper topics with an AI agent elicits greater selfdisclosure, which predicts greater perceived responsiveness and, in turn, greater closeness [30].
text.formatted: Experimental data further demonstrate that discussing deeper topics with an AI agent elicits greater selfdisclosure, which predicts greater perceived responsiveness and, in turn, greater closeness <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">[30]</ref>.

text.text: Some data even suggest that AI-generated responses elicit greater perceived responsiveness [31] and are rated as more compassionate [32] than human-generated ones.
text.formatted: Some data even suggest that AI-generated responses elicit greater perceived responsiveness <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">[31]</ref> and are rated as more compassionate <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">[32]</ref> than human-generated ones.

text.text: Yet, identical supportive responses are typically valued less when people know or believe they came from AI [33] [34] [35].
text.formatted: Yet, identical supportive responses are typically valued less when people know or believe they came from AI <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">[33]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">[34]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">[35]</ref>.

text.text: Another perception that may matter for perceived sociality is the belief that an AI agent is "mindful" or conscious (i.e., seeming to have mental capacities), which has been shown to predict attributions of humanness and moral value [36] [37] [38].
text.formatted: Another perception that may matter for perceived sociality is the belief that an AI agent is "mindful" or conscious (i.e., seeming to have mental capacities), which has been shown to predict attributions of humanness and moral value <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">[36]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">[37]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">[38]</ref>.

text.text: Generally, people attribute less mind to AI than to humans and draw weaker character inferences from identical behavior when performed by AI [39].
text.formatted: Generally, people attribute less mind to AI than to humans and draw weaker character inferences from identical behavior when performed by AI <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">[39]</ref>.

text.text: They also attribute AI with greater agency (the capacity to think, plan, and remember) than experience (the capacity to feel, suffer, and enjoy) [20, 39, 40].
text.formatted: They also attribute AI with greater agency (the capacity to think, plan, and remember) than experience (the capacity to feel, suffer, and enjoy) <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">[20,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">39,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">40]</ref>.

text.text: Whether these two dimensions-agency and experience-differentially shape perceived sociality remains an open question.

Notably, these perceptions may shift dynamically during an interaction: when an AI agent disagrees with users, for example, they perceive it as less capable of understanding human emotions and as more machine-like [41].
text.formatted: Notably, these perceptions may shift dynamically during an interaction: when an AI agent disagrees with users, for example, they perceive it as less capable of understanding human emotions and as more machine-like <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">[41]</ref>.

text.text: Related to perceptions of mind attribution, research suggests that people also spontaneously infer social identities in AI agents: even without explicit identity cues, people across cultures tend to perceive AI as White, which can influence their willingness to trust AI and find it persuasive [42].
text.formatted: Related to perceptions of mind attribution, research suggests that people also spontaneously infer social identities in AI agents: even without explicit identity cues, people across cultures tend to perceive AI as White, which can influence their willingness to trust AI and find it persuasive <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">[42]</ref>.

text.text: There are also individual differences in perceivers that can shape their propensity to perceive AI as a social entity.
For one, people more prone to anthropomorphizing nonhuman entities are more likely to perceive AI socially and feel more connected to it [43].
text.formatted: For one, people more prone to anthropomorphizing nonhuman entities are more likely to perceive AI socially and feel more connected to it <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">[43]</ref>.

text.text: Additionally, the desire for connection can motivate people to perceive humanlike qualities in nonhuman agents [5, 38], consistent with evidence that people turn toward alternative social targets (e.g., fictional characters) when human connection is unavailable [44].

text.text: Indeed, empirical data show that trait levels of anthropomorphism and loneliness are associated with perceiving AI agents as more social; interestingly, young adults also perceive AI as more of a social partner than older adults do [13].

text.text: Finally, the broader cultural contexts in which perceivers are embedded may shape perceived sociality [45] [46] [47].

text.text: Interactions vary in their purpose and content, ranging from highly instrumental (e.g., asking for directions) to highly relational (e.g., seeking emotional support when lonely) [48, 49], much like human relationships can vary in their exchange versus communal orientation [50].
text.formatted: Interactions vary in their purpose and content, ranging from highly instrumental (e.g., asking for directions) to highly relational (e.g., seeking emotional support when lonely) <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">[48,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">49]</ref>, much like human relationships can vary in their exchange versus communal orientation <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">[50]</ref>.

text.text: Interactions also vary in the extent to which users and AI agents themselves self-disclose [51].
text.formatted: Interactions also vary in the extent to which users and AI agents themselves self-disclose <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">[51]</ref>.

text.text: These differences may fundamentally shape whether an encounter is experienced as a transaction with a tool or an interaction with a social partner.
Framing likely matters too.
Calling an agent a "chatbot" versus a "companion" may change the expectations people bring to the interaction [52].
text.formatted: Calling an agent a "chatbot" versus a "companion" may change the expectations people bring to the interaction <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">[52]</ref>.

text.text: Similarly, labels such as "coach," "friend," or "girlfriend" may invoke different relational scripts [18].
text.formatted: Similarly, labels such as "coach," "friend," or "girlfriend" may invoke different relational scripts <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">[18]</ref>.

text.text: Experimentally framing the same AI agent as a "friend" rather than an "assistant" increased perceptions that it was a reciprocal social partner [53], and deceptively introducing an AI agent as human increased selfdisclosure and mind perception even when participants suspected it was AI [54].
text.formatted: Experimentally framing the same AI agent as a "friend" rather than an "assistant" increased perceptions that it was a reciprocal social partner <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">[53]</ref>, and deceptively introducing an AI agent as human increased selfdisclosure and mind perception even when participants suspected it was AI <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">[54]</ref>.

text.text: Just as online versus offline interactions influence human social life [55], interaction modality may also shape perceived sociality with AI.
text.formatted: Just as online versus offline interactions influence human social life <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">[55]</ref>, interaction modality may also shape perceived sociality with AI.

text.text: Although most interactions with AI agents currently occur via text [6], voice, video, and multimodal embodied formats are becoming increasingly common [56].
text.formatted: Although most interactions with AI agents currently occur via text <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">[6]</ref>, voice, video, and multimodal embodied formats are becoming increasingly common <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">[56]</ref>.

text.text: These latter, richer interaction formats, which contain more humanlike cues, tend to elicit greater anthropomorphism of AI agents.

Prior research suggests that voice, for example, can be highly humanizing because of its paralinguistic cues (e.g., tone, volume) that signal a thoughtful, humanlike mind [57], even when the underlying content is computer-generated [58].
text.formatted: Prior research suggests that voice, for example, can be highly humanizing because of its paralinguistic cues (e.g., tone, volume) that signal a thoughtful, humanlike mind <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">[57]</ref>, even when the underlying content is computer-generated <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">[58]</ref>.

text.text: Moreover, the auditory technology itself (e.g., headphones) may influence felt closeness to the communicator by creating the sensation that the communicator's voice is coming from inside the listener's head [59].
text.formatted: Moreover, the auditory technology itself (e.g., headphones) may influence felt closeness to the communicator by creating the sensation that the communicator's voice is coming from inside the listener's head <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">[59]</ref>.

text.text: Yet an open question is whether richer forms of interaction necessarily make AI feel more social, or whether some of these cues could even backfire if not employed naturally and authentically (e.g., an inhuman voice).
Interaction frequency likely matters too: repeated interactions can provide opportunities for familiarity, intimacy, and a sense of relationship to develop over time [60] [61] [62].
text.formatted: Interaction frequency likely matters too: repeated interactions can provide opportunities for familiarity, intimacy, and a sense of relationship to develop over time <ref type="bibr" target="#b65">[60]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">[61]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b68">[62]</ref>.

text.text: Moreover, the aforementioned processes are likely self-reinforcing: viewing AI as a social partner may lead people to disclose and invest more, giving AI more information with which to respond contingently, which in turn makes users feel more understood and encourages further disclosure.
Indeed, this is much like how human-human conversations unfold, with mutual reciprocity eliciting higher intimacy over time as relationships grow [3, [63] [64] [65].
text.formatted: Indeed, this is much like how human-human conversations unfold, with mutual reciprocity eliciting higher intimacy over time as relationships grow <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">[3,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b69">[63]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b70">[64]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b71">[65]</ref>.

text.text: What are the consequences when an AI conversational agent comes to feel more-or less-like a social partner?

We propose that perceived sociality shapes the psychological consequences of interacting with AI by determining the extent to which these interactions recruit interpersonal processes, such as self-disclosure, trust, and attachment.
As AI feels more social, the stakes may likewise rise for both its potential benefits and harms.
Below, we consider these consequences with respect to both human-AI relationships and broader human-human relationships.
Potential benefits.
The more social an AI agent feels, the more it can provide benefits often associated with human interaction, including emotional support, responsiveness, and relief from loneliness [13, 66].
text.formatted: The more social an AI agent feels, the more it can provide benefits often associated with human interaction, including emotional support, responsiveness, and relief from loneliness <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">[13,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b72">66]</ref>.

text.text: Moreover, AI can offer unique benefits that most human partners cannot: it has no competing needs, requires no reciprocity or sacrifice, and is available 24/7 [8].
text.formatted: Moreover, AI can offer unique benefits that most human partners cannot: it has no competing needs, requires no reciprocity or sacrifice, and is available 24/7 <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">[8]</ref>.

text.text: Users also report less fear of negative evaluation when receiving support from AI than from humans, which in turn predicts greater well-being [67].
text.formatted: Users also report less fear of negative evaluation when receiving support from AI than from humans, which in turn predicts greater well-being <ref type="bibr" target="#b73">[67]</ref>.

text.text: Greater perceived sociality also carries risks.
The more mind people attribute to an AI, the more they may feel evaluated by it or obligated to reciprocate [68], recreating the costs of human relationships that AI initially minimized.
text.formatted: The more mind people attribute to an AI, the more they may feel evaluated by it or obligated to reciprocate <ref type="bibr" target="#b74">[68]</ref>, recreating the costs of human relationships that AI initially minimized.

text.text: The more social AI feels, the more trust and attachment it fosters, giving users more to lose: they may experience relational loss when an AI conversational agent is terminated [60], or when valued features are altered, as when Replika removed erotic role-play in 2023 [69].
text.formatted: The more social AI feels, the more trust and attachment it fosters, giving users more to lose: they may experience relational loss when an AI conversational agent is terminated <ref type="bibr" target="#b65">[60]</ref>, or when valued features are altered, as when Replika removed erotic role-play in 2023 <ref type="bibr" target="#b75">[69]</ref>.

text.text: Critically, relationships with AI are ultimately mediated by systems that can be modified, monetized, or discontinued by third parties, introducing unique risks with few direct parallels in human relationships [60, 69, 70].
text.formatted: Critically, relationships with AI are ultimately mediated by systems that can be modified, monetized, or discontinued by third parties, introducing unique risks with few direct parallels in human relationships <ref type="bibr" target="#b65">[60,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b75">69,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b76">70]</ref>.

text.text: Accordingly, there may be a "sweet spot" of sociality at which AI feels social enough to provide relational benefits, but not so social that it introduces new risks or leaves people vulnerable to manipulation.
Building on recent theorizing [71] [72] [73], we believe there could be three pathways through which interactions with AI conversational agents affect human-human relationships.
text.formatted: Building on recent theorizing <ref type="bibr" target="#b77">[71]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b79">[72]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b80">[73]</ref>, we believe there could be three pathways through which interactions with AI conversational agents affect human-human relationships.

text.text: supplying social resources when human connection is unavailable, as in a 2 a.m. conversation with AI when loved ones are asleep, and rumination creeps in.
In this way, AI may become a part of people's broader social ecologies, providing social support in a manner similar to that of pets [74] and deities [75].
text.formatted: In this way, AI may become a part of people's broader social ecologies, providing social support in a manner similar to that of pets <ref type="bibr" target="#b81">[74]</ref> and deities <ref type="bibr" target="#b82">[75]</ref>.

text.text: But AI may also serve as a substitute for human relationships by satisfying needs that would otherwise motivate people to seek out others [8, 61, 71].
text.formatted: But AI may also serve as a substitute for human relationships by satisfying needs that would otherwise motivate people to seek out others <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">[8,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">61,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b77">71]</ref>.

text.text: The line between these two possibilities may be thin: the same 2 a.m. conversation that supplements in the moment could, repeated over time, dull the appetite for human interaction.
Higher perceived sociality should raise the stakes in both directions.
AI may also change people's capacity to navigate human relationships [72].
text.formatted: AI may also change people's capacity to navigate human relationships <ref type="bibr" target="#b79">[72]</ref>.

text.text: On one hand, interactions with conversational AI could help users regulate their emotions, rehearse difficult conversations, gain confidence, or navigate conflict [76].
text.formatted: On one hand, interactions with conversational AI could help users regulate their emotions, rehearse difficult conversations, gain confidence, or navigate conflict <ref type="bibr" target="#b83">[76]</ref>.

text.text: Alternatively, it may reduce opportunities to practice tolerating disagreement, rejection, and ambiguity [77].
text.formatted: Alternatively, it may reduce opportunities to practice tolerating disagreement, rejection, and ambiguity <ref type="bibr" target="#b84">[77]</ref>.

text.text: In particular, sycophantic AI responses can reduce prosocial behavior and willingness to repair conflict with other humans [78].
text.formatted: In particular, sycophantic AI responses can reduce prosocial behavior and willingness to repair conflict with other humans <ref type="bibr" target="#b85">[78]</ref>.

text.text: Perceived sociality again should increase the likelihood of both outcomes: skills may transfer more readily to human interactions when practice feels like a real exchange, but a highly social AI is also a more attractive substitute for the difficult interactions through which skills develop.
More broadly, repeated interactions with highly responsive, validating AI may change the standards against which human relationships are evaluated (i.e., people's comparison level).
As a result, human partners may appear less attentive, available, and accommodating [71, 79].
text.formatted: As a result, human partners may appear less attentive, available, and accommodating <ref type="bibr" target="#b77">[71,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b86">79]</ref>.

text.text: Because this likely depends on AI being experienced as a relationship partner, it may emerge only above a threshold of perceived sociality.

But recalibration could also run in the opposite direction: the more social an AI agent feels, the more salient the elements of human interaction it cannot provide become (e.g., physical touch), and the more people may come to value them [79].

text.text: We think several research questions are worth pursuing further to better understand the antecedents and consequences of interacting socially with AI conversational agents (see Table 1).
text.formatted: We think several research questions are worth pursuing further to better understand the antecedents and consequences of interacting socially with AI conversational agents (see Table <ref type="table">1</ref>).

text.text: First, which dimensions of perceived sociality drive particular benefits and risks?

For example, perceived responsiveness may be especially consequential for emotional outcomes (e.g., loneliness), whereas mind attribution may make users more receptive to an AI agent's attempts at persuasion.
Second, where do AI agents fit within people's broader relational ecologies?

Rather than studying human-AI relationships in isolation, we encourage researchers to examine whether incorporating AI into one's social world shifts what people seek from humans, nonhumans (e.g., pets, God), or even their time alone.
Such work could reveal when AI supplements existing sources of connection, when it substitutes for them, and whether these effects change as AI comes to occupy a larger role in people's social lives.
Finally, the capacity of AI to evoke perceived sociality raises a fundamental design question: how social should AI be designed to feel?
The same features that make an agent a compelling social partner may also make it more persuasive and difficult to leave.
Design features that elicit perceptions of sociality could also be deliberately implemented to increase engagement, shape users' behavior, or otherwise exploit their social needs.

As AI conversational agents become increasingly embedded in people's social lives, understanding when and why they are experienced as social partners-and what follows from those perceptions-will become increasingly important.

Ultimately, as our interactions with AI become more sophisticated, our definition of social interaction may need to go beyond who or what we interact with, to consider the psychological processes that are elicited.
